newsitem.title: CHINA: China says fuel surcharge issue unresolved.
newsitem.headline: China says fuel surcharge issue unresolved.

text.p: China's newly approved highway law states that a fuel surcharge should replace road maintenance taxes but the State Council still needs to study implementation procedures, officials said on Friday.

The law, which takes effect on January 1 next year, states that a fuel surcharge should be imposed to replace such road fees but the plan has aroused considerable opposition, officials told reporters.
Article 36 of the law, approved by parliament recently, says that individuals and government agencies that own cars should pay a fuel surcharge according to relevant state regulations.
It also says that once this is in effect, road maintenance fees should no longer be collected, though it specifically leaves further measures to be set by the State Council, or cabinet.
Since 1994, the island of Hainan off China's southern coast has instituted a 60 percent surcharge on gasoline as a way of replacing tolls and vehicle registration fees.
But the surcharge has led to widespread smuggling and opposition from powerful special interest groups within the province, officials said.
Military vehicles, for example, do not pay registration fees but are subject to the fuel surcharge. China's military wields considerable political and economic clout.
"We still need the State Council to study the implementation procedures," said Wu Fuzhao, a senior economist and member of parliament who helped draft the new law.
"As of now there is no change in existing fees," he told reporters.
Other officials said there were further issues to be addressed such as whether to tax diesel use.
"This affects agricultural vehicles and agriculture is a very sensitive issue," said Xu Ruqing of the Communications Ministry.
